name: Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort
positioning: Eco-resort of traditional Fijian-style bures on a peninsula in Savusavu Bay, on Fiji's island of Vanua Levu, with diving, snorkeling and a free kids club
best_for: Divers and snorkelers who want reef sites close by
Families who want a free kids club and a teen program

facts.text: The resort sits on a peninsula surrounded by Savusavu Bay.
The resort is on Vanua Levu, Fiji's northern island, near the town of Savusavu.
The resort is set on 17 acres overlooking Savusavu Bay, less than a 15-minute drive from downtown Savusavu.
Jean-Michel Cousteau, son of ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau, discovered the property in the 1980s and gave the resort his name.
The resort's design is inspired by a traditional Fijian village.
The bures have vaulted, exposed-beam ceilings with woven magimagi, a coconut fiber rope.
The bures have no phones or televisions, but there is Wi-Fi.
The Dreamhouse dive site has barracudas, grey reef sharks and white tip sharks and is recommended for seasoned divers.
The Golden Nugget site is a calm, shallow protected area suited to snorkelers.
The spa offers traditional Fijian Bobo massage.
A teen program offers reef conservation, cultural storytelling and waterfall hikes.
A traditional Fijian lovo feast is prepared once a week.

highlights.text: Divers can visit the Namena Marine Reserve, known for coral biodiversity, large fish populations, hawksbill turtles and seasonal whale migrations.
Resident marine biologists lead snorkeling expeditions and presentations on Savusavu Bay's marine ecology.
The Oceanfront Point Reef Spa Tub Bure has a private spa tub on the deck with views of Point Reef Beach.
The Kids Bula Club is free for all guests.
The Premium Oceanfront Two-Bedroom Villa has its own pool and spa tub.

considerations.text: Getting there takes two flights: international flights arrive at Nadi, then guests take a domestic flight to Savusavu and a 20-minute transfer by road.
The spa is small: the beachfront spa bure has two oceanfront, open-air treatment rooms.
There are no adapted bures, but paths are paved and ramps reach public areas.
